lessons.title: Exact ratios, quadrants and principal inverse values
lessons.summary: Use exact values and coordinate signs, then distinguish a principal inverse value from every solution.
lessons.objective: Find exact sine, cosine and tangent values for general angles and interpret inverse trigonometric notation correctly.
lessons.before: Recall right-triangle ratios, Pythagoras and conversion between degrees and radians.
lessons.ideas:
Exact values come from two triangles

Bisect an equilateral triangle to obtain the 30° and 60° ratios; use an isosceles right triangle for 45°. In radian measure:

\[\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&\frac\pi6&\frac\pi4&\frac\pi3\\\hline\sin x&\frac12&\frac{\sqrt2}2&\frac{\sqrt3}2\\\cos x&\frac{\sqrt3}2&\frac{\sqrt2}2&\frac12\\\tan x&\frac{\sqrt3}3&1&\sqrt3\end{array}\]

General angles use coordinates and signs

On the unit circle the point is \((\cos x,\sin x)\). Anticlockwise rotation is positive. Reduce by complete turns, identify the reference angle, then choose the sign from the quadrant. Tangent is \(\sin x/\cos x\), so it is undefined when \(\cos x=0\).

An inverse value uses a specified branch

\[\sin^{-1}t\in\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right],\]\[\cos^{-1}t\in[0,\pi],\qquad\tan^{-1}t\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right).\]

The inputs of inverse sine and cosine must lie in \([-1,1]\). Inverse tangent accepts every real input. The notation \(\sin^{-1}t\) means a principal angle, not \(1/\sin t\). An equation can have other angles outside that principal range.

Composition does not erase the branch restriction

Although \(\sin(\sin^{-1}t)=t\) for an allowed input, \(\sin^{-1}(\sin x)\) need not equal x outside the principal interval. Check units and calculator mode.
lessons.method:
1. State the angle unit and reduce complete turns.
  2. Find the reference angle and the quadrant signs.
  3. Use exact ratios or Pythagoras, keeping the required signs.
  4. For an inverse, select its principal branch; for an equation, return to the full stated interval.

The written questions combine these skills with algebra, identities and transformed-angle equations later in this chapter.
mistakes: An inverse function is not a reciprocal.
A square root gives a magnitude; the quadrant fixes its sign.
An inverse calculator value is not automatically the full solution set.
Keep radians and degrees distinct.

examples.title: Reference angles and signs
examples.question: Find \(\sin(7\pi/6)\), \(\cos(7\pi/4)\) and \(\tan(2\pi/3)\) exactly.
examples.solution:
The reference angles are π/6, π/4 and π/3. The signs are respectively negative, positive and negative.

\[\sin\frac{7\pi}{6}=-\frac12,\qquad\cos\frac{7\pi}{4}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\]\[\tan\frac{2\pi}{3}=-\sqrt3.\]

examples.title: Pythagoras with a quadrant
examples.question: Given \(\cos\theta=-5/13\) and \(\pi<\theta<3\pi/2\), find \(\sin\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\).
examples.solution:
\[\sin^2\theta=1-\frac{25}{169}=\frac{144}{169}.\]

Quadrant III makes sine negative and tangent positive:

\[\sin\theta=-\frac{12}{13},\qquad\tan\theta=\frac{12}{5}.\]

examples.title: Choose the principal value
examples.question: Find \(\sin^{-1}(-\sqrt3/2)\), \(\cos^{-1}(-1/2)\) and \(\tan^{-1}(-1)\) in radians.
examples.solution:
Use each inverse relation’s own output interval:

\[\sin^{-1}\!\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=-\frac\pi3,\]\[\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac12\right)=\frac{2\pi}{3},\qquad\tan^{-1}(-1)=-\frac\pi4.\]

For example, 4π/3 has the required sine but is not the principal inverse-sine value.

examples.title: An inverse inside a composition
examples.question: Evaluate \(\sin(\cos^{-1}(\frac35))\) and \(\sin^{-1}(\sin(\frac{5\pi}6))\).
examples.solution:
If \(\alpha=\cos^{-1}(\frac35)\), then α is acute. A right triangle gives \(\sin\alpha=\frac45\). For the other expression \(\sin(\frac{5\pi}6)=\frac12\), whose principal inverse-sine value is \(\frac\pi6\).

\[\sin(\cos^{-1}(\tfrac35))=\frac45,\]\[\sin^{-1}(\sin(\tfrac{5\pi}6))=\frac\pi6.\]

lessons.title: Trigonometric graphs, periods and transformations
lessons.summary: Read a full cycle, distinguish inside and outside changes and keep tangent branches separate.
lessons.objective: Sketch and interpret sine, cosine and tangent graphs, including scale factors, shifts, ranges and asymptotes.
lessons.before: Recall function transformations, radian measure and exact values.
lessons.ideas:
Start with the three basic shapes

Sine starts at zero; cosine starts at one. Both have range \([-1,1]\) and period 2π. Tangent has period π, takes all real values and has separate branches divided by vertical asymptotes.

Separate the midline, scale and input

For \(y=a\sin(bx+c)+d\) or its cosine counterpart, with a and b nonzero, the amplitude is |a|, the midline is y=d and the range is \([d-|a|,d+|a|]\).

\[T=\frac{2\pi}{|b|},\qquad bx+c=b\left(x+\frac cb\right).\]

The horizontal shift to the right is \(-c/b\). A negative value means a shift to the left. Degree-mode periods use 360° in place of 2π.

Tangent has no amplitude

For \(y=a\tan(bx+c)+d\), the period is \(\pi/|b|\). Find asymptotes by solving \(bx+c=\pi/2+k\pi\). Do not join branches across an asymptote.

Transform the entire input

A horizontal stretch by h>0 maps \((x,y)\) to \((hx,y)\) and changes f(x) to f(x/h). Reflection in the y-axis uses f(−x). Apply the same change to every term, including a linear term outside a trigonometric function.
lessons.method:
1. Choose a unit and mark one complete cycle.
  2. Identify midline, amplitude where defined, period and horizontal shift.
  3. Plot key points or asymptotes, then repeat only within the stated domain.
  4. Use intersections to count solutions; do not assume a restricted arc repeats beyond its domain.
mistakes: The horizontal scale factor is the reciprocal of the input coefficient.
The shift in sin(bx+c) is not simply −c.
A negative amplitude coefficient reflects the curve; amplitude itself is non-negative.
Tangent has no amplitude and no point at an asymptote.

examples.title: Read the vertical and horizontal information
examples.question: For \(y=2-3\cos2x\), state the amplitude, period and range. Find its maxima for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
examples.solution:
The midline is 2 and the vertical scale has magnitude 3.

\[\text{amplitude}=3,\quad T=\pi,\quad -1\le y\le5.\]

A maximum occurs when cos 2x=−1, giving x=π/2 and 3π/2. Its value is 5.

examples.title: Factor the input before reading the shift
examples.question: Describe \(y=2\sin(3x-\pi/2)+1\) and locate five key points in a cycle starting at its rising midline crossing.
examples.solution:
\[3x-\pi/2=3(x-\pi/6).\]

The shift is π/6 right, period 2π/3, amplitude 2 and midline 1. Quarter-period spacing is π/6.

\[(\pi/6,1),\ (\pi/3,3),\ (\pi/2,1),\]\[(2\pi/3,-1),\ (5\pi/6,1).\]

examples.title: A tangent branch has endpoints it never reaches
examples.question: For \(y=1-2\tan(x/2)\), give its period, y-intercept and the asymptotes bordering the branch containing x=0.
examples.solution:
\[T=\frac\pi{1/2}=2\pi,\qquad y(0)=1.\]

The neighbouring asymptotes satisfy x/2=±π/2, so x=−π and x=π. The branch decreases and its range is all real numbers. It has no amplitude.

examples.title: Every term and the point use the same map
examples.question: The curve \(y=f(x)=x+\cos x\) is reflected in the y-axis, then stretched horizontally by factor 2. Find its equation and the image of \((\pi,\pi-1)\).
examples.solution:
The new input is −x/2, so

\[y=f(-x/2)=-\frac x2+\cos\frac x2.\]

The point map is (a,b)→(−2a,b), giving (−2π,π−1). Substituting its x-coordinate into the new equation gives the same ordinate.

lessons.title: Identities, algebra and valid domains
lessons.summary: Use the two basic identities and retain every restriction from the original expression.
lessons.objective: Prove and simplify identities using Pythagoras, factorisation and common denominators without extending the original domain.
lessons.before: Recall factorisation, fractions and the meaning of a denominator restriction.
lessons.ideas:
Two identities do most of the work

\[\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1,\qquad\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}.\]

The first holds for every real angle; the second requires cos x≠0. For example, dividing the first identity by cos²x gives \(1+\tan^2x=1/\cos^2x\) on that domain.

Choose one side and transform it

Rewrite tangent as a ratio, factor a difference of squares or combine fractions. Aim for the other side with justified equalities. Checking several numerical angles does not prove an identity.

Cancellation preserves exclusions

The expression \((1-\cos^2x)/\sin x\) simplifies to sin x where sin x≠0. Its simplified appearance does not supply values at the excluded angles. Likewise, multiplying an equation by a denominator is valid only after recording where it is nonzero.

Identity and equation ask different questions

An identity is true for every input in its stated common domain. An equation asks for the inputs where equality holds. Prove the identity first; when using it to solve an equation, return to the original restrictions.
lessons.method:
1. Record the original denominators and excluded inputs.
  2. Choose the more complicated side and rewrite using sine and cosine.
  3. Factor or combine fractions, explaining each equality.
  4. State the domain of the result; check excluded candidates separately when solving.
mistakes: Do not give a cancelled denominator a value of zero.
An identity needs an algebraic argument, not just examples.
sin²x means (sin x)²; it is not sin(x²).
You can use sin²x+cos²x=1 without a double-angle formula.

examples.title: The simplified value still has a domain
examples.question: Simplify \((1-\cos^2x)/\sin x\) and give its excluded inputs on \([0,2\pi]\).
examples.solution:
\[\frac{1-\cos^2x}{\sin x}=\frac{\sin^2x}{\sin x}=\sin x\quad(\sin x\ne0).\]

The original expression excludes x=0, π and 2π. It is not defined there, even though sin x itself is.

examples.title: Multiply by a conjugate
examples.question: Prove \((1-\sin x)/\cos x=\cos x/(1+\sin x)\) on its common domain.
examples.solution:
Require cos x≠0. This also rules out sin x=−1. Then

\[\frac{1-\sin x}{\cos x}=\frac{(1-\sin x)(1+\sin x)}{\cos x(1+\sin x)}\]\[=\frac{\cos^2x}{\cos x(1+\sin x)}=\frac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}.\]

The two expressions agree on their common domain; neither equality authorises a cancelled input.

examples.title: Reduce fourth powers without extra identities
examples.question: Express \(\sin^4x-\cos^4x\) as a polynomial in \(u=\sin x\).
examples.solution:
\[\sin^4x-\cos^4x=(\sin^2x-\cos^2x)(\sin^2x+\cos^2x)\]\[=\sin^2x-\cos^2x=2u^2-1.\]

Only factorisation and the basic Pythagorean identity were needed.

examples.title: A tangent identity with its restriction
examples.question: Prove \((1+\tan^2x)\cos^2x=1\) and state where the original left side is defined.
examples.solution:
\[(1+\tan^2x)\cos^2x=\left(1+\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}\right)\cos^2x\]\[=\cos^2x+\sin^2x=1.\]

The original expression requires cos x≠0. At x=π/2+kπ, tangent is undefined, so the displayed value 1 cannot be assigned to that original expression.

lessons.title: All solutions on a stated interval
lessons.summary: Find every branch, transform the interval with the angle and keep zero factors.
lessons.objective: Solve sine, cosine and tangent equations on open, closed or half-open intervals, including shifted and multiple angles.
lessons.before: Recall exact ratios, inverse branches, graph periods, factorisation and inequalities.
lessons.ideas:
One inverse value is a starting point

For sin u=c, solutions come from \(u=\alpha+2k\pi\) or \(u=\pi-\alpha+2k\pi\), where α=sin⁻¹c. For cos u=c, use \(u=\pm\beta+2k\pi\), where β=cos⁻¹c. For tan u=c, use \(u=\gamma+k\pi\), where γ=tan⁻¹c. Here k is an integer.

Transform the interval before enumerating angles

If u=bx+c, apply the same map to the interval for x, reversing endpoint order if b<0. Find every allowed u, then recover \(x=(u-c)/b\). A doubled input can cross more than one cycle even when x does not.

Factor before dividing

In sin x(2cos x−1)=0, keep both sin x=0 and 2cos x−1=0. Dividing by sin x would discard valid solutions.

Endpoints are part of the question

Check each candidate against the original interval and denominators. Angles 0 and 2π are different inputs when both endpoints are included. List each distinct allowed input once, preferably in increasing order.
lessons.method:
1. Write the interval and angle unit, including endpoint brackets.
  2. Factor if possible or isolate one trigonometric ratio.
  3. Transform the interval with the input angle and enumerate all branches.
  4. Recover x, discard invalid inputs and check the original equation.
mistakes: Do not stop after the principal inverse value.
Transform the interval as well as the angle.
Never divide away a factor which may be zero.
Include or exclude 0, π and 2π according to the actual interval.

examples.title: Both branches belong in the answer
examples.question: Solve \(\sin x=\sqrt3/2\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
examples.solution:
The principal angle is π/3. Sine is positive in quadrants I and II, so

\[x=\frac\pi3,\quad\frac{2\pi}{3}.\]

Neither endpoint satisfies the equation, and the sine graph has no further intersection in the interval.

examples.title: A shifted input includes three branches
examples.question: Solve \(\cos(2x-\pi/3)=1/2\) for \(0\le x\le\pi\).
examples.solution:
Set u=2x−π/3, so −π/3≤u≤5π/3. Cos u=1/2 gives u=−π/3, π/3 and 5π/3 in that interval.

\[x=\frac{u+\pi/3}{2}=0,\quad\frac\pi3,\quad\pi.\]

Both endpoints satisfy the original equation and must be retained.

examples.title: Tangent repeats after a half-turn
examples.question: Solve \(\tan(x+\pi/4)=-1\) for \(-\pi\le x<\pi\).
examples.solution:
\[x+\frac\pi4=-\frac\pi4+k\pi,\qquad x=-\frac\pi2+k\pi.\]

The interval selects x=−π/2 and π/2. At both inputs tangent’s argument is defined and its value is −1.

examples.title: Keep the factor that can equal zero
examples.question: Solve \(\sin x(2\cos x-1)=0\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
examples.solution:
The first factor gives x=0 or π. The second gives cos x=1/2, hence x=π/3 or 5π/3.

\[x\in\{0,\pi/3,\pi,5\pi/3\}.\]

The upper endpoint 2π is excluded. Dividing by sin x would lose the first two solutions.

lessons.title: Trigonometric quadratics and complete angle sets
lessons.summary: Solve the algebra, reject impossible ratio values and recover every permitted angle.
lessons.objective: Reduce trigonometric equations to polynomials and distinguish algebraic roots, admissible ratios and angle solutions.
lessons.before: Recall quadratic methods, the two Pythagorean identities, graph ranges and interval enumeration.
lessons.ideas:
Name the ratio you are solving for

Let u=sin x, cos x or tan x as appropriate. Rewrite the equation as a polynomial in u; use factorisation, completing the square or the quadratic formula. When both sine and cosine occur, try \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\) or its counterpart.

Filter algebraic roots before finding angles

For u=sin x or cos x retain only −1≤u≤1. Tangent has no such range bound, but its original input must be defined. A repeated algebraic root is not an extra angle; a single admissible ratio can give several angles.

Return to the original interval

For a multiple or shifted angle, transform the interval before enumerating. Treat a squared ratio as two possible signs when its value is positive. Check denominator restrictions and substitute candidates into the original equation.

A graph explains why counts differ

For example, the quadratic \(3u^2+2u-1=0\) has roots u=1/3 and −1. If u=cos x on \([0,2\pi)\), the first level gives two angles and the second gives one.
lessons.method:
1. Choose one ratio and derive its polynomial equation.
  2. Solve all algebraic roots, showing the method.
  3. Apply ratio ranges and original denominator restrictions.
  4. Enumerate every permitted angle, restore x and verify all candidates.
mistakes: A polynomial root outside [−1,1] cannot be a sine or cosine.
A squared ratio has two signs unless its value is zero.
Two polynomial roots need not give two angle solutions.
A multiple input changes the interval and the number of cycles.

examples.title: Two algebraic roots give three angles
examples.question: Solve \(3\cos^2x+2\cos x-1=0\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\). Give exact answers.
examples.solution:
Let u=cos x. Then

\[3u^2+2u-1=(3u-1)(u+1)=0.\]

Both u=1/3 and −1 are allowed. Put α=cos⁻¹(1/3), with 0<α<π/2. Then

\[x=\alpha,\quad\pi,\quad2\pi-\alpha.\]

The diagram’s two cosine levels explain the three distinct inputs.

examples.title: An algebraic root outside the ratio range
examples.question: Solve \(2\sin^2x-5\sin x+2=0\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
examples.solution:
\[(2\sin x-1)(\sin x-2)=0.\]

Sin x=2 is impossible. Sin x=1/2 gives

\[x=\pi/6,\quad5\pi/6.\]

Rejecting an impossible ratio is different from forgetting a second trigonometric branch.

examples.title: Use the identity to choose one variable
examples.question: Solve \(3\sin^2x+4\cos x-4=0\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
examples.solution:
Set u=cos x and replace sin²x by 1−u²:

\[3(1-u^2)+4u-4=0,\qquad(3u-1)(u-1)=0.\]

Thus u=1/3 or 1. With α=cos⁻¹(1/3), the complete answer is

\[x=0,\quad\alpha,\quad2\pi-\alpha,\quad2\pi.\]

Both endpoints are included and are distinct inputs.

examples.title: Restore both signs before halving the input
examples.question: Solve \(4\sin^2(2x)-1=0\) for \(0\le x<\pi\).
examples.solution:
Put u=2x, so 0≤u<2π. Then sin²u=1/4 gives sin u=±1/2.

\[u=\pi/6,\ 5\pi/6,\ 7\pi/6,\ 11\pi/6.\]

Halve each input, not just the first:

\[x=\pi/12,\ 5\pi/12,\ 7\pi/12,\ 11\pi/12.\]

questions.title: Three exact signed ratios
questions.prompt_html: Find \(\sin(\frac{7 \pi}{6})\), \(\cos(\frac{5 \pi}{4})\), \(\tan(\frac{2 \pi}{3})\) exactly.
questions.solution_html:
Reduce to reference angles π/6, π/4 or π/3, then use the quadrant to set each sign. Keep the values exact.

Complete answers

Sine value: \(- \frac{1}{2}\)

Cosine value: \(- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\)

Tangent value: \(- \sqrt{3}\)
questions.hint_html: Use an exact reference angle and the required quadrant or principal branch.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Sine value.
Complete correct answer for Cosine value.
Complete correct answer for Tangent value.

questions.title: Pythagoras with signed ratios
questions.prompt_html: Given \(\cos\theta=- \frac{5}{13}\) and θ in quadrant 3, find sin θ and tan θ exactly.
questions.solution_html:
\[\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta.\]

Both stated quadrants have negative sine. Select that sign, then divide sine by cosine for tangent.

Complete answers

sin θ: \(- \frac{12}{13}\)

tan θ: \(\frac{12}{5}\)
questions.hint_html: Use an exact reference angle and the required quadrant or principal branch.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for sin θ.
Complete correct answer for tan θ.

questions.title: Principal inverse values
questions.prompt_html: Give the principal radian values of \(\sin^{-1}(- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})\), \(\cos^{-1}(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})\), \(\tan^{-1}(- \sqrt{3})\).
questions.solution_html:
Use the ranges [−π/2,π/2], [0,π] and (−π/2,π/2), respectively. Choose each branch before simplifying.

Complete answers

Inverse sine (radians): \(- \frac{\pi}{4}\)

Inverse cosine (radians): \(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\)

Inverse tangent (radians): \(- \frac{\pi}{3}\)
questions.hint_html: Use an exact reference angle and the required quadrant or principal branch.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Inverse sine (radians).
Complete correct answer for Inverse cosine (radians).
Complete correct answer for Inverse tangent (radians).

questions.title: Inverse is not reciprocal
questions.prompt_html: What does the −1 in \(\sin^{-1}t\) mean? Then evaluate \(\sin^{-1}(\sin(\frac{5 \pi}{6}))\) in radians.
questions.answer_html:
Meaning of inverse notation: The principal inverse-sine angle

Principal result (radians): \(\frac{\pi}{6}\)
questions.solution_html:
Inverse sine returns the angle in its principal interval. First evaluate the sine, then find that angle; the starting input may lie outside the principal range.

Complete answers

Meaning of inverse notation: The principal inverse-sine angle

Principal result (radians): \(\frac{\pi}{6}\)
questions.hint_html: Use an exact reference angle and the required quadrant or principal branch.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Meaning of inverse notation.
Complete correct answer for Principal result (radians).

questions.title: Amplitude, period and full range
questions.prompt_html: For \(y=-3\cos(2x)+2\), give the amplitude, period in radians, minimum and maximum.
questions.solution_html:
The vertical scale magnitude is the amplitude, the midline is the constant term, and the input coefficient divides the basic 2π period. Add and subtract the amplitude from the midline.

Complete answers

Amplitude: \(3\)

Period (radians): \(\pi\)

Minimum value: \(-1\)

Maximum value: \(5\)
questions.hint_html: Separate inside and outside changes; a tangent graph has asymptotes rather than an amplitude.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Amplitude.
Complete correct answer for Period (radians).
Complete correct answer for Minimum value.
Complete correct answer for Maximum value.

questions.title: Factor the input to find the shift
questions.prompt_html: For \(y=2\sin(3x- \frac{\pi}{2})+1\), give the horizontal shift to the right, period and midline. A negative shift means left.
questions.solution_html:
\[bx+c=b(x+c/b).\]

The shift is −c/b, not −c. The period is 2π/|b| and the midline is the outside constant.

Complete answers

Horizontal shift to the right (radians): \(\frac{\pi}{6}\)

Period (radians): \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\)

Midline y-value: \(1\)
questions.hint_html: Separate inside and outside changes; a tangent graph has asymptotes rather than an amplitude.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Horizontal shift to the right (radians).
Complete correct answer for Period (radians).
Complete correct answer for Midline y-value.

questions.title: Tangent has an open central branch
questions.prompt_html: For \(y=2\tan(3x)-1\), give the domain interval of the branch containing x=0, its period and its y-intercept.
questions.solution_html:
The neighbouring poles satisfy bx=±π/2 and are excluded. Tangent’s period is π/|b|, and tan 0=0.

Complete answers

Central branch interval: \((- \frac{\pi}{6},\, \frac{\pi}{6})\)

Period (radians): \(\frac{\pi}{3}\)

y-intercept: \(-1\)
questions.hint_html: Separate inside and outside changes; a tangent graph has asymptotes rather than an amplitude.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Central branch interval.
Complete correct answer for Period (radians).
Complete correct answer for y-intercept.

questions.title: A point and the complete input map
questions.prompt_html: A point \(\left( \frac{\pi}{3}, \ 2\right)\) lies on y=f(x). Reflect the curve in the y-axis, then stretch it horizontally by factor \(2\). Give the image point and k in the new equation y=f(kx).
questions.solution_html:
The point map is (a,b)→(−ha,b), whereas the input coefficient is −1/h. The coordinate map and the substitution have reciprocal scale factors.

Complete answers

Image point (x,y): \(\left(- \frac{2 \pi}{3},\, 2\right)\)

Input coefficient k: \(- \frac{1}{2}\)
questions.hint_html: Separate inside and outside changes; a tangent graph has asymptotes rather than an amplitude.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Image point (x,y).
Complete correct answer for Input coefficient k.

questions.title: A simplification keeps its exclusions
questions.prompt_html: Simplify \(\frac{1-\cos^2x}{\sin x}\) as a polynomial in \(u=\sin x\). Give every excluded x in \([0,2\pi]\).
questions.solution_html:
The numerator is the square of the denominator’s trigonometric ratio. Cancel only when that ratio is nonzero, keeping the original excluded angles.

Complete answers

Simplified expression in u: \(u\)

Excluded x-values (radians): \(\{0,\, \pi,\, 2 \pi\}\)
questions.hint_html: Rewrite with the two basic identities and retain original denominator exclusions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Simplified expression in u.
Complete correct answer for Excluded x-values (radians).

questions.title: Reduce powers before finding zeros
questions.prompt_html: Express \(\sin^4x-\cos^4x\) as a polynomial in u=sin x. Then give all its zeros in \([0,2\pi)\).
questions.solution_html:
Factor a difference of squares and use sin²x+cos²x=1. Solve the resulting ratio condition, retaining every sign and quadrant.

Complete answers

Polynomial in u: \(2 u^{2} - 1\)

All zero inputs (radians): \(\{\frac{\pi}{4},\, \frac{3 \pi}{4},\, \frac{5 \pi}{4},\, \frac{7 \pi}{4}\}\)
questions.hint_html: Rewrite with the two basic identities and retain original denominator exclusions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Polynomial in u.
Complete correct answer for All zero inputs (radians).

questions.title: A rationalised form has a common domain
questions.prompt_html: Select an equivalent form of \((1-\sin x)/\cos x\) on its original domain. Give all excluded inputs in \([0,2\pi]\).
questions.solution_html:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate 1 plus the same ratio, then use the Pythagorean identity. Keep the original denominator restriction.

Complete answers

Equivalent expression: \(\cos x/(1+\sin x)\)

Excluded x-values (radians): \(\{\frac{\pi}{2},\, \frac{3 \pi}{2}\}\)
questions.hint_html: Rewrite with the two basic identities and retain original denominator exclusions.

options.A: The original expression is defined for every real x

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Equivalent expression.
Complete correct answer for Excluded x-values (radians).

questions.title: A cancelled factor leaves missing inputs
questions.prompt_html: For \(F(x)=\frac{\sin x(\cos x-\frac{1}{2})}{\cos x-\frac{1}{2}}\), give its simplified expression in u=sin x and its excluded x-values on \([0,2\pi)\). What is the original F at a zero of the cancelled factor?
questions.answer_html:
Simplified expression in u: \(u\)

Excluded x-values (radians): \(\{\frac{\pi}{3},\, \frac{5 \pi}{3}\}\)

Original value at an excluded input: Undefined
questions.solution_html:
Cancel the common factor only on the original domain. The factor’s zero angles remain excluded; the original fraction is not defined there.

questions.title: Inside changes and outside changes
questions.prompt_html:
For real x in radians,

\[f(x)=2 \cos{\left(x \right)} + 1,\quad g(x)=f(2x)+3,\quad h(x)=-2f(x+\pi).\]

  1. Describe a sequence taking y = f(x) to y = g(x).

    [2]

  2. Describe a sequence taking y = f(x) to y = h(x). State the range of h.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

A horizontal stretch of factor 1/2, followed by translation \(\left( 0, \ 3\right)\).

(b)

Translate left by \(\pi\), reflect in the x-axis, and stretch vertically by factor 2. Range: \(-6\leq y\leq 2\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

questions.title: Transforming a restricted sine arc
questions.prompt_html:
Only the part of \(y=\sin x\) with \(0\leq x\leq \frac{\pi}{2}\) is used. It is transformed to

on the corresponding transformed domain. Angles are in radians.

    [4]

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

Stretch horizontally by \(3\), vertically by \(2\), then translate upwards by \(1\). Domain \(0\leq x\leq \frac{3 \pi}{2}\), range \(1\leq y\leq 3\).

(b) \(\frac{\pi}{2}\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Each input coordinate is multiplied by 1/m. The original restricted sine arc is increasing from 0 to 1, so the transformed arc runs from \(1\) to \(3\).

(b)

The transformed angle lies in \(0\leq x\leq \frac{\pi}{2}\), where sine is one-to-one. The unique angle is π/6.
questions.hint_html: The original right endpoint π/2 is stretched horizontally too.

questions.title: Reading a phase and a period
questions.prompt_html:
The diagram shows \(y=\sin(a(x+b))\), with a > 0 and b > 0. A maximum occurs at \(\left( \frac{\pi}{3}, \ 1\right)\) and the next descending zero is \(\left( \frac{5 \pi}{6}, \ 0\right)\). Angles are in radians.

  1. Find a and the smallest positive possible value of b.

    [3]

  2. Find all x in \(0\leq x\leq 2 \pi\) for which y = 1/2.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The descending zero follows the maximum by a quarter-period. Their separation is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), so the period is \(2 \pi\). Thus a = \(1\). At the maximum, \(a(x+b)=\frac{\pi}{2}\) modulo a full turn; use the smallest positive shift.

(b)

Use both sine branches on the full argument interval, including its endpoints.

questions.title: Principal inverse notation before a double input
questions.prompt_html:
The inverse tangent is its principal value. Find t from

\[\frac{\pi}{6}+\tan^{-1}(3 t + 1)=-\cos^{-1}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}).\]

  1. Find t exactly and justify the inverse-tangent angle used.

    [2]

  2. Using this value of t, solve \(\tan(2x)=3 t + 1\) for \(0^\circ\leq x\leq 180^\circ\). Give degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The principal inverse cosine is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\), so the inverse tangent must be \(- \frac{\pi}{3}\). This lies strictly between −π/2 and π/2. Thus \(3 t + 1=- \sqrt{3}\) and \(t=- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} - \frac{1}{3}\).

(b)

The angle 2x runs from 0 to 2π, so both tangent branches must be considered.
questions.hint_html: An inverse symbol gives one principal value; an equation with tan may have several.

questions.title: Principal inverse notation before a double input
questions.prompt_html:
The inverse tangent is its principal value. Find t from

\[\frac{\pi}{6}+\tan^{-1}(5 t - 1)=-\cos^{-1}(1).\]

  1. Find t exactly and justify the inverse-tangent angle used.

    [2]

  2. Using this value of t, solve \(\tan(2x)=5 t - 1\) for \(0^\circ\leq x\leq 180^\circ\). Give degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The principal inverse cosine is \(0\), so the inverse tangent must be \(- \frac{\pi}{6}\). This lies strictly between −π/2 and π/2. Thus \(5 t - 1=- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\) and \(t=\frac{1}{5} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{15}\).

(b)

The angle 2x runs from 0 to 2π, so both tangent branches must be considered.

questions.title: The sign is part of the exact value
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(\alpha=\cos^{-1}(- \frac{3}{5})\), with inverse cosine taking its principal value.

  1. Without evaluating an angle numerically, find \(\frac1{\sin\alpha}+1\frac1{\tan\alpha}\) exactly.

The principal inverse cosine places α in quadrant II. Thus sin α is positive and equals \(\frac{4}{5}\), while tan α is negative. Substitute these signed exact ratios.

(b)

questions.title: A shifted cosine and a principal inverse relation
questions.prompt_html:
A curve has equation

\[y = 2 \sin{\left(x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\]

for \(\frac{\pi}{6}\leq x\leq \frac{13 \pi}{6}\). Angles are in radians.

  1. Find the first zero after x = \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) and the following minimum.

    [3]

  2. Find t exactly from \(2\sin^{-1}(3t)+2\cos^{-1}(\frac12)=\pi\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

From a cosine maximum, the first zero is a quarter-period later and the minimum is a half-period later. The period is 2π.

(b)

The principal inverse cosine is π/3. Hence the inverse sine equals \(\frac{\pi}{6}\), which is in its principal range. Take sine and divide by \(3\).
questions.hint_html: A positive-amplitude cosine starts at its maximum when its argument is zero.

questions.title: A reciprocal cosine with an inadmissible algebraic root
questions.prompt_html:
Solve

\[2 \cos{\left(x \right)} - 5 + \frac{2}{\cos{\left(x \right)}}=0\]

for \(-90^\circ<x<90^\circ\). Give angles to 1 decimal place.

  1. Derive a polynomial equation in \(u\), stating the substitution, its range and all original denominator restrictions.

    [2]

  2. Hence find every solution of the original equation in the stated interval.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \[2 u^{2} - 5 u + 2 = 0\]

\(u=\cos(x)\), \(-1\leq u\leq1\). Original restrictions: \(\cos{\left(x \right)}\ne0\).

(b) \(-60.0^\circ\), \(60.0^\circ\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

questions.title: An acute solution after changing the ratio
questions.prompt_html:
Solve

\[3 \cos{\left(x \right)} - 8 \tan{\left(x \right)}=0\]

for \(0^\circ<x<90^\circ\). Give angles to 1 decimal place.

  1. Derive a polynomial equation in \(u\), stating the substitution, its range and all original denominator restrictions.

    [3]

  2. Hence find every solution of the original equation in the stated interval.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \[3 u^{2} + 8 u - 3 = 0\]

\(u=\sin(x)\), \(-1\leq u\leq1\). Original restrictions: \(\cos{\left(x \right)}\ne0\).

(b) \(19.5^\circ\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(u=\sin(x)\), with \(-1\leq u\leq1\). Use tan x = sin x/cos x and multiply by the non-zero cosine. The original acute condition chooses the positive sine target.

\[3 u^{2} + 8 u - 3 = 0\]

The real algebraic candidates are \(\frac{1}{3}\), \(-3\).

(b)

Keep only ratio values in the trigonometric range. Use every branch in the stated interval, then undo the angle change \(w=x\). Apply each original denominator restriction.

Ratio targetPermitted x-values (degrees)
\(\frac{1}{3}\)\(19.5^\circ\)
\(-3\)Outside the range [−1,1].

The complete solution set is \(19.5^\circ\).

questions.title: A cosine endpoint and an independent discriminant
questions.prompt_html:
Solve

\[2 \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(x \right)} + 1=0\]

for \(0^\circ\leq x\leq 180^\circ\). Give angles to 1 decimal place.

  1. Derive a polynomial equation in \(u\), stating the substitution, its range and all original denominator restrictions.

    [1]

  2. Hence find every solution of the original equation in the stated interval.

    [3]

  3. For this independent algebraic equation, find all real k for which \(k u + 2 u^{2} + 1=0\) has no real roots.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \[2 u^{2} - 3 u + 1 = 0\]

\(u=\cos(x)\), \(-1\leq u\leq1\).

(b) \(0.0^\circ\), \(60.0^\circ\)
(c) \(-2 \sqrt{2}<k<2 \sqrt{2}\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(u=\cos(x)\), with \(-1\leq u\leq1\). One cosine target is exactly 1, so it contributes the endpoint x = 0.

\[2 u^{2} - 3 u + 1 = 0\]

The real algebraic candidates are \(\frac{1}{2}\), \(1\).

(b)

Keep only ratio values in the trigonometric range. Use every branch in the stated interval, then undo the angle change \(w=x\). Apply each original denominator restriction.

Ratio targetPermitted x-values (degrees)
\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(60.0^\circ\)
\(1\)\(0.0^\circ\)

The complete solution set is \(0.0^\circ\), \(60.0^\circ\).

(c)

The leading coefficient is positive. The discriminant is k² − 4n, so require k² < 4n, with strict endpoints.

questions.title: A cosine square and an exact parameter threshold
questions.prompt_html:
Solve

\[2 \cos^{4}{\left(x \right)} + 3 \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)} - 2=0\]

for \(0\leq x\leq 2 \pi\). Give exact answers.

  1. Derive a quadratic equation in \(u\), stating the substitution, its range and all original denominator restrictions.

    [2]

  2. Hence find every solution of the original equation in the stated interval.

    [3]

  3. For \(f_k(x)=2\cos^4x+3\cos^2x-k\), find all real k for which fₖ(x) = 0 has no solution on [0,2π].

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \[2 u^{2} + 3 u - 2 = 0\]

\(u=\cos^2(x)\), \(0\leq u\leq1\).

(b) \(\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\), \(\frac{5 \pi}{4}\), \(\frac{7 \pi}{4}\)
(c) \(k<0\quad\text{or}\quad k>5\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(u=\cos^2(x)\), with \(0\leq u\leq1\). First solve in w = cos² x. The two w-roots are \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(-2\). Retain 0 ≤ w ≤ 1, then use both cosine signs.

\[2 u^{2} + 3 u - 2 = 0\]

The real algebraic candidates are \(-2\), \(\frac{1}{2}\). Keep the allowed squared ratio, then recover both signs of the ratio itself.

(b)

Keep only ratio values in the trigonometric range. Use every branch in the stated interval, then undo the angle change \(w=x\). Apply each original denominator restriction.

Ratio targetPermitted x-values (radians)
\(- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\)\(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\), \(\frac{5 \pi}{4}\)
\(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\)\(\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\frac{7 \pi}{4}\)

The complete solution set is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\), \(\frac{5 \pi}{4}\), \(\frac{7 \pi}{4}\).

(c)

Put w = cos² x ∈ [0,1]. Both terms Aw² and Bw increase on this interval, so Aw² + Bw ranges from 0 to A + B, with both endpoints attained. Outside that closed range there is no solution.

questions.title: A cancelled factor leaves a missing input
questions.prompt_html:
The expression is

\[\frac{\sin^{2}{\left(x \right)} - \cos{\left(x \right)} - 1}{\cos{\left(x \right)} + 1}\]

for all angles where it is defined.

  1. Prove \(\frac{\sin^{2}{\left(x \right)} - \cos{\left(x \right)} - 1}{\cos{\left(x \right)} + 1}\equiv-\cos x\) and explain why the simplified expression does not restore the original excluded point.

    [3]

  2. Hence solve \(- \frac{1}{4} + \frac{\sin^{2}{\left(x \right)} - \cos{\left(x \right)} - 1}{2 \left(\cos{\left(x \right)} + 1\right)}=0\) on \(0^\circ\leq x\leq 360^\circ\). Give angles to 1 decimal place.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \[\frac{\sin^{2}{\left(x \right)} - \cos{\left(x \right)} - 1}{\cos{\left(x \right)} + 1}\equiv -\cos x\]

The original expression is undefined where cos x = −1.

(b) \(120.0^\circ\), \(240.0^\circ\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Replace sin² x by 1 − cos² x. The numerator is −cos x(1 + cos x). Cancellation is valid only when 1 + cos x ≠ 0; the missing point remains excluded.

(b)

The identity reduces the equation to cos x = \(- \frac{1}{2}\). Neither returned angle is an excluded point.
questions.hint_html: An identity is valid on a common domain; cancellation does not enlarge it.

marking_criteria.description_html: Uses the Pythagorean identity.
Factors and cancels on the common domain.
Retains the original excluded input.
Uses the simplified cosine equation.
Uses both cosine branches.
Complete domain-checked answers.

questions.title: A parameter range with a missing value
questions.prompt_html:
The original relation is

\[\frac{\sin{\left(x \right)} + \tan{\left(x \right)}}{- \sin{\left(x \right)} + \tan{\left(x \right)}}=k.\]

  1. Express cos x in terms of k, retaining the original domain restrictions.

    [3]

  2. Find the complete set of possible real k for the original relation, for real x.

    [2]

  3. For \(k=2\), solve the original relation on \(- \pi<x<\pi\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Replace tangent by sine/cosine. Cancel sine only after noting it is non-zero in the original denominator, obtaining (1 + cos x)/(1 − cos x) = k. Rearrange; k = −1 is impossible.

(b)

The original relation excludes sin x = 0 and cos x = 0. Therefore cos x lies in (−1,1) with 0 removed. Its rational image is positive, with k = 1 removed. Each remaining k corresponds to a permitted cosine.

(c)

The cosine target is \(\frac{1}{3}\). Use the two symmetric angles in the centred interval and verify the original denominator.

questions.title: A ratio mixing tangent and cosine
questions.prompt_html:
Solve

\[-2 + \frac{\cos{\left(x \right)} + \tan{\left(x \right)}}{- \cos{\left(x \right)} + \tan{\left(x \right)}}=0\]

for \(0^\circ\leq x\leq 360^\circ\). Give angles to 1 decimal place.

  1. Derive a polynomial equation in \(u\), stating the substitution, its range and all original denominator restrictions.

    [3]

  2. Hence find every solution of the original equation in the stated interval.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \[3 u^{2} + u - 3 = 0\]

\(u=\sin(x)\), \(-1\leq u\leq1\). Original restrictions: \(\cos{\left(x \right)}\ne0\), \(- \cos{\left(x \right)} + \tan{\left(x \right)}\ne0\).

(b) \(57.9^\circ\), \(122.1^\circ\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(u=\sin(x)\), with \(-1\leq u\leq1\). Convert tan x to sin x/cos x, then use cos² x = 1 − sin² x. One quadratic root lies below −1 and must be rejected.

\[3 u^{2} + u - 3 = 0\]

questions.title: A supplied factorisation unlocks a rational equation
questions.prompt_html:
You may use the factorisation

\[8 u^{3} - 4 u + 1=\left(2 u - 1\right) \left(4 u^{2} + 2 u - 1\right)\]

  1. Verify the supplied factorisation by expansion.

    [1]

  2. Prove \(\frac{\tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 1}{\tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} - 1}\equiv \frac{1}{1 - 2 \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}}\), stating its common domain.

    [3]

  3. Hence solve \(- 4 \cos{\left(x \right)} + \frac{\tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 1}{\tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} - 1}=0\) on \(0^\circ\leq x\leq 180^\circ\). Give degrees to 1 decimal place.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \[8 u^{3} - 4 u + 1=\left(2 u - 1\right) \left(4 u^{2} + 2 u - 1\right)\]
(b) \[\frac{\tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 1}{\tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} - 1}\equiv \frac{1}{1 - 2 \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}}\]
(c) \(60.0^\circ\), \(72.0^\circ\), \(144.0^\circ\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Expand the right side, or divide the cubic by its known factor \(u - \frac{1}{2}\). The coefficients agree.

Multiply numerator and denominator by cos² x. The numerator becomes 1 and the denominator becomes \(1-2\cos^2x\). Retain cos x ≠ 0 and tan² x ≠ \(1\).

(c)

The identity gives the cubic in cos x displayed above. Use the supplied factorisation, solve the remaining quadratic, reject any cosine outside [−1,1], and check every original denominator.
